title: WHY IS AN ENTIRE BOOK OF ROMANTIC DESIRE SITTING BETWEEN ECCLESIASTES AND ISAIAH?
paragraphs: WHY IS AN ENTIRE BOOK OF ROMANTIC DESIRE SITTING BETWEEN ECCLESIASTES AND ISAIAH?

The Bible could have moved from Solomon’s search for meaning straight into Isaiah’s thunderous visions of holiness. Instead, right in the middle, God preserved a song filled with kisses, perfume, longing, beauty, bodies, absence, desire, marriage, and a love so fierce it is compared with death. Why? Maybe because God refuses to surrender one of the deepest parts of being human to the enemy.
There is a moment when an honest Bible reader reaches the Song of Songs and quietly wonders what nobody in church taught them to ask.
What is this doing here?
You have just walked through Ecclesiastes.
“Vanity of vanities.”
Death.
Time.
Work.
Regret.
Meaning.
The aching realization that everything under the sun eventually slips through our fingers.
Then you turn the page...
And suddenly someone wants to be kissed.
The Hebrew does not soften it.
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth...” — Song of Songs 1:2.
That is not a mistranslation.
That is Scripture.
The book opens with שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים — Shir haShirim — “Song of Songs.” The construction functions like a superlative: not merely a song, but the supreme song, the song among songs.
And immediately, it begins with desire.
No apology.
No embarrassment.
No attempt to pretend human beings do not have bodies.
No nervous religious cough before changing the subject.
Then, after this astonishing collection of longing and delight, the Bible moves into Isaiah:
“Holy, holy, holy.”
So why is a book of romantic desire sitting there?
Why would God preserve poetry about attraction, longing, beauty, exclusivity, marriage, absence, reunion and desire inside Holy Scripture?
Perhaps the question underneath the question is even more uncomfortable:
What if God is not embarrassed by something the church has sometimes been embarrassed to discuss?
And what if the enemy has been extraordinarily successful at corrupting precisely what God intended to be received with holiness, covenant, gratitude and joy?
Because sexuality was not invented by pornography.
Desire was not invented by Hollywood.
The human body was not invented by lust.
Marriage was not invented by culture.

Long before sin distorted desire, God created humanity male and female. Long before pornography commercialized bodies, Genesis declared the naked husband and wife unashamed. Long before adultery fractured homes, God established covenant. Long before lust whispered, “Take what does not belong to you,” God created a love capable of saying, “I belong to my beloved.”
That sentence appears in the Song itself:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְדוֹדִי לִי
Ani le-dodi ve-dodi li.
“I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.” — Song of Songs 6:3.
Read it again.
Not consumption.
Belonging.
Not exploitation.
Mutuality.
Not anonymous bodies using each other for temporary relief.
Covenantal language of giving and receiving.
This matters because many people reading this know what it feels like when desire stops feeling beautiful.
Some know what it is to have pornography sitting in browser history while a Bible sits on the nightstand.
Some know what it is to be married and lonely.
Some know what it is to have given their body to someone who promised permanence and disappeared.
Some know what it is to wake up beside somebody and somehow feel more alone than when the bed was empty.
Some have confused attention with love.
Some have accepted manipulation because they were starving to feel wanted.
Some learned sexuality from screens before anyone taught them holiness.
Some were wounded by somebody else's sinful desire.
Some carry memories they desperately wish they could erase.
Some have repented repeatedly and still wonder whether Jesus is disgusted with them.
And some became so ashamed of desire itself that they quietly began believing holiness meant becoming less human.
Then Song of Songs sits in the Bible like a protest.
God does not redeem us by teaching us to hate His creation.
He redeems what sin has distorted.
That distinction changes everything.

The Song should not be reduced to an ancient Christian code in which every vineyard, breast, fragrance, kiss and garden secretly means something else. Its plain literary surface celebrates the passionate love of a man and woman. Christian tradition has also long read the Song spiritually, while the New Testament itself uses marriage and bridegroom imagery for Christ and His people. The responsible Christ-centered reading therefore does not have to erase human love in order to see where the whole biblical story eventually leads.
The Bible can celebrate covenant love between husband and wife...
and then show us that marriage itself ultimately points beyond itself.
Paul does exactly that in Ephesians 5.
He speaks about husband and wife, then suddenly opens a window into something infinitely larger:
Christ and His Church.
Human marriage is real.
Human desire within its God-given covenant is real.
But even the most faithful marriage cannot carry the weight of being somebody's savior.
Your husband cannot redeem your soul.
Your wife cannot cleanse your sin.
Romance cannot resurrect you.
Sex cannot give you eternal life.
Being desired cannot finally tell you who you are.
There is a hunger underneath our hungers that another human being cannot permanently satisfy.
And that is where the love story becomes breathtaking.
Because the Gospel does not announce that humanity climbed its way back to God.
It announces that God came looking for humanity.
Jesus Christ entered our shame.
He touched people respectable religion avoided.
He ate with sinners.
He received the broken.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people to repentance.
He carried our sin to a Roman cross.
And there, the One who had no scandal of His own was publicly crucified beneath ours.
Our lust.
Our adultery.
Our pornography.
Our secret messages.
Our betrayal.
Our pride.
Our religious pretending.
Our selfishness.
Our attempts to turn people into objects.
Our desperate search for love in places that could never love us back.
He bore sin—not so we could rename darkness and remain inside it, but so sinners could be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled and transformed.
That is grace.
Grace is not Jesus looking at sin and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace is Jesus looking at a sinner and saying, in effect, “Your sin mattered enough for Me to bleed for it, and I love you enough not to leave you enslaved to it.”
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the moment you finally stop defending the prison whose door Christ has opened.
Maybe that is why this book feels so dangerous.
Because beneath all its perfume and poetry is a truth our generation desperately needs:
Love is not casual.
Love has weight.
Song of Songs eventually erupts with one of Scripture's most staggering descriptions of it:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-azzah khamavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death...” — Song of Songs 8:6.
Then comes an extraordinary expression:
שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה
shalhevetyah.

A blazing flame—an expression traditionally understood as “a flame of Yah,” or an intensely mighty flame. The Hebrew imagery refuses to describe love as harmless sentimentality. It burns. It claims. It costs. It cannot simply be purchased like merchandise.
And suddenly our culture's version of “love” begins looking painfully thin.
Swipe.
Use.
Hide.
Delete.
Replace.
Repeat.
But biblical love keeps moving toward covenant.
Toward faithfulness.
Toward giving.
Toward belonging.
Toward sacrifice.
And when Scripture reaches its fullest revelation of sacrificial love, we do not find perfume.
We smell blood.
We do not find a garden of romantic celebration.
We first find another garden where Jesus sweats in anguish and says yes to the Father's will.
Then we find a cross.
The Bridegroom loves His people at unimaginable cost.
Christ does not merely desire a beautiful bride.
He gives Himself to make His people holy.
That is why the Gospel is not the story of beautiful people finally becoming worthy enough for Jesus.
It is the story of Jesus giving Himself for sinners and making a people His own.
Scandal becomes grace.
Shame meets mercy.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
The wandering are called home.
The unclean are washed.
The spiritually dead are offered life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have been calling yourself by the name of your worst chapter.
Cheater.
Addict.
Used.
Dirty.
Rejected.
Divorced.
Unwanted.
Porn addict.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Too far gone.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not save you by pretending your past never happened.
He does something greater.
He refuses to let your past have the final word.
At the cross, sin is exposed as terrible enough to require the death of the Son of God.
At the resurrection, grace is revealed as powerful enough that death itself cannot keep the final word.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Redemption.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace writing an ending the scandal could never produce.
And perhaps now we begin understanding why Song of Songs belongs in the Bible.
Because God cares about what we love.
God cares about how we desire.
God cares about how husbands and wives treat each other.
God cares about bodies because He created bodies.
God cares about fidelity because He is faithful.
God cares about covenant.
God cares about wounded hearts.
God cares about the person who feels unwanted.
God cares about the person fighting sexual temptation at 2:17 in the morning when nobody else knows.
God cares about the marriage that has become cold.
God cares about the single Christian who wonders whether waiting is worth it.
God cares about the person whose boundaries were violated and whose understanding of intimacy was wounded by someone else's sin.
God cares about the believer ashamed to admit that this battle is still a battle.
And Jesus is not calling you merely to behavior modification.
He wants your heart.
That is where Christianity becomes painfully personal.
You can delete the app and still crave validation.
You can install the filter and still worship desire.
You can stop sleeping with someone and still secretly make that person your god.
You can be technically sexually pure and remain consumed by pride.
You can wear a wedding ring and be emotionally unfaithful.
You can quote Scripture while starving your spouse of tenderness.
You can condemn the sexual sins everybody can see while carefully protecting the lust nobody can.
Jesus did not come merely to polish the outside of religious people.
He came to make dead hearts alive.
So be honest.
What are you actually hungry for?
To be touched?
To be chosen?
To be noticed?
To be wanted?
To be told you are beautiful?
To know someone will stay?
Those longings can become disordered, but their existence may reveal something painfully human.
We ache to be known without being abandoned.
And here the Gospel reaches deeper than romance ever can.
God already knows.
The secret.
The browser history.
The fantasy.
The betrayal.
The loneliness.
The night you never told anybody about.
The thing done to you.
The thing you did.
The prayer you stopped praying.
The marriage nobody knows is struggling.
The addiction hidden beneath Christian language.
The tears after everyone went to sleep.
He knows.
And the invitation of Christ is not, “Clean yourself until I can tolerate you.”
It is:
Repent.
Come.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Me.
Be made new.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already carried you out of a place you thought would destroy you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed to survive tonight.
This is why Gospel truth must keep traveling.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Because temptation has a way of returning after conviction fades.
Loneliness returns.
Shame starts talking again.
Old names come knocking.
And you may need to remember:
your hunger is not your master.
your history is not your savior.
your sexuality is not your identity.
your shame does not own you.
Jesus Christ is Lord.

Scripture allows those who proclaim the Gospel to receive material support for Gospel work, while also teaching that Christian giving must never be extracted through pressure or compulsion; it should come willingly from the heart. Salvation cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel ministry continue.
It should be the mission.
If this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life and you want to help that Gospel-centered work reach farther, prayerfully consider becoming one of the people who helps carry it.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Follow and invite others to follow so they can continue receiving Scripture-centered encouragement.
Because perhaps that is the final surprise hidden inside the Song of Songs.
The Bible contains a song of desire because the God who created us is not interested only in the polished religious pieces of us.
He claims the whole person.
Mind.
Body.
History.
Desire.
Wounds.
Relationships.
Failures.
Future.
He enters places shame told us to hide.
He confronts what sin distorted.
He forgives what repentance brings into the light.
He restores what can be restored.
He teaches us to love without consuming.
To desire without worshiping desire.
To belong without possessing another person as an idol.
To see bodies without turning people into objects.
To understand marriage without making marriage a savior.
And finally...
to discover that beneath every lesser longing is the question eternity keeps asking:
What happens when the thing you have been searching for in human arms can finally be found only in the pierced hands of Christ?
Maybe your story has scandal in it.
Maybe more than anybody knows.
But if you bring that story to Jesus, the scandal does not get to write the final sentence.
Grace does.
The chapter you are most ashamed to reread may become the very page where someone else discovers what Jesus can redeem.
